messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Elena Weber is a 73-year-old forester who came to treatment after decades of living in careful, constricted routines that had begun to collapse under the strain of retirement planning and increasing time indoors alone. She grew up in a rural household where a female caregiver repeatedly physically abused her behind closed doors. What has remained most vivid is not a single incident but the pattern: being trapped alone in a room with a woman whose face was close to hers, the sound of footsteps or a voice approaching, and, just as often, the strange drop into complete silence before the first blow. As a child, Elena learned to wait inside that silence, certain that harm could arrive without warning. Even now, what frightens her most is the sense that you can never know who will harm you, and that in those moments she ceased to be a person at all and became something to be handled, pinned down, and hurt.

Over the years she had come to believe that the abuse had ruined the course of her life. Divorced and living alone, she spoke in a flat, matter-of-fact way about having “lost the chance to be normal,” and said that the trauma had destroyed her life before it had properly begun. That belief shaped how she read the present. Being alone with women could feel immediately dangerous to her, even in ordinary situations, because she was certain threat could hide behind familiarity and caretaking. The presence of a female colleague in a closed office at the forestry station, or a woman lingering with her in a supply shed, could bring a hard jolt of alarm. Certain related sounds—women’s footsteps in a hall, a voice outside a door, the small domestic noises that once signaled someone coming toward her—had a similar force. So did sudden silence. In the woods, the abrupt hush after birdsong stopped could make her body brace before she had consciously understood why.

Because Elena saw the world through this expectation of hidden danger, she had built her life around not being exposed. At work she preferred tasks that kept her moving across open tracts rather than paperwork in the district office, and she would rearrange schedules so she did not have to be alone in a room or building. If she had to stop at headquarters, she often lingered in doorways or found an excuse to keep another person nearby. She also stopped most forms of exercise years ago. She said exercise made her too aware of her body and breath, and she disliked anything that left her feeling physically vulnerable or confined to an indoor class with women around her. On difficult evenings she drove to town and bought gardening tools, jackets, kitchen items she did not need, describing the spending as the quickest way to blot things out for an hour or two. These habits made sense to her as protection, given how completely she believed her life had already been wrecked and how little reason she felt she had to trust anyone.

Yet the ways Elena tried to manage herself seemed to deepen the very beliefs she lived by. Avoiding being alone in rooms or buildings left her increasingly convinced that such situations truly were unsafe, and each time she escaped one she felt a grim confirmation that vigilance was all that stood between her and being hurt. Giving up exercise contributed to her sense of herself as diminished and trapped in a body that was not fully hers, which fed the old feeling of being an object rather than a person. The impulsive spending brought brief comfort, but afterward she would look at unopened purchases and feel ashamed, telling herself this was further evidence of what the trauma had done to her life. The more her routines narrowed, the easier it became for her to think in absolute terms: that harm could come from anyone, that she had been permanently altered, that there was no real self left underneath the habits.

Those same strategies also kept her triggers close at hand. By refusing to be alone in buildings, Elena monitored constantly for whether she might end up trapped with a woman in an enclosed space, which made female presence more charged, not less. Avoiding exercise meant she spent more time in sedentary, indoor settings where ordinary household sounds and stretches of silence stood out sharply. Shopping to distract herself often placed her in stores crowded with women’s voices, footsteps, and changing pockets of sound and hush that she found hard to bear. Even in the forest, where she had once felt most competent, she had started choosing routes based on who else might be around rather than on the work itself, listening tensely for sounds behind her and dreading the blank, sudden quiet that still felt like a warning.

She finally sought help after realizing she was considering leaving a profession she had loved because the office had hired a new female administrator. Elena noticed herself timing her visits to avoid being alone with the woman and sitting in her truck until someone else entered the building. What frightened her was not only the intensity of the fear, but the conviction that at 73 she was still living as if the abuse were waiting just outside the door. What she hopes for, cautiously, is not to erase the past but to stop organizing every room, every silence, and every encounter around the certainty of being harmed again.
